segments: 191. The 11th Jubilee.
Hunnic (Mongol) Kings.
and fulfilled all his requests.
Because an order had previously gone out that churches should be destroyed,
King Het‘um requested of the King of Kings that the churches not be destroyed,
because they are the courts of God
and moreover houses of prayer.
And so the King of Kings commanded that they should not be destroyed,
and he wrote a sigillion (patent) and sent messengers that churches should not be destroyed at all,
but only the temples of idols should be overturned,
and mosques and schools of study should belong to the Muslims.
And so, by the hands of this faithful king, many churches were saved from destruction. And this same king departed from the camp with a pleasant heart, rejoicing and exulting,
on Sunday, the ninth
of the First Tishri, in this year, which is the beginning of the year 1607
of the Greeks (1295 of our Lord). Immediately, suddenly and unexpectedly, that Nawruz attacked him (Baydu) with troops,
in a place called Qungur-Olan.
Baydu, however, was not able to hold out for even one hour before the King of Kings, Ghazan, nor to face him or meet him at all,
but quickly turned his back
and fled before him (Nawruz) on Saturday,
on the 25th (24th)
of the month of Elul in the year
[1606]. And when that Nawruz pursued after him,
he overtook him and killed him on Thursday, the sixth of the First Tishri [1607].
And he issued an order that churches, idol temples, and synagogues of the Jews should be destroyed,
and that the priests (of idolaters) should be killed,
and the chief priests humiliated,
and tribute and poll taxes should be imposed upon them;
and that no Christian should be seen unless his loins were bound with a girdle (zunara),
nor a Jew, unless with a sign upon his head.
And in those same days,
the pagans (Muslims) laid hands in Tabriz
and destroyed all the churches that were there.
And there was great mourning for the Christians throughout the whole world.
Moreover, the persecution, dishonour, contempt, and insult that the Christians endured at this time,
the spoken word is unable to circumscribe,
especially in Baghdad.
For behold, as they say,
no Christian dared to be seen outside in the street,
but only women went out and in, and bought and sold,
since they could not be distinguished from the Muslim women,
nor recognized.
